\section{Results}
\label{sec:results}

We evaluate depth fingerprinting along four axes: cross-generator classification (\S\ref{sec:results-classification}), differential depth response of individual features (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}), comparison with existing detection baselines (\S\ref{sec:results-baselines}), and downstream utility for data curation (\S\ref{sec:results-downstream}).

\subsection{Depth Classification Performance}
\label{sec:results-classification}

Table~\ref{tab:logo-results} reports leave-one-generator-out (LOGO) macro-F1 for 3-class depth estimation (gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+) across six generators spanning three model families and parameter counts from 0.6B to 8.2B.

The 7-feature ensemble achieves LOGO F1\,=\,0.790 (95\% bootstrap CI [0.786, 0.799]), significantly outperforming all single-detector baselines ($p<0.001$; \S\ref{sec:results-baselines}).
Per-generator held-out F1 ranges from 0.685 (Qwen3-8B) to 0.855 (Pythia-1B).
Gen-0 classification is near-perfect (per-class F1\,$\approx$\,0.95); the primary difficulty lies in distinguishing gen-1 from gen-2+, where feature margins narrow.

\paragraph{Cross-scale transfer.}
The six-generator evaluation includes Qwen3-8B (8.2B parameters), confirming that depth signal persists at scales beyond the $\leq$2.8B training generators.
However, cross-scale transfer incurs a moderate gap: Qwen3-8B held-out F1\,=\,0.685 (CI [0.672, 0.698]), compared to 0.76--0.86 for $\leq$2.8B generators.
Text generated by larger models is more fluent, compressing feature margins and making depth distinctions harder.
Notably, adding Qwen3-8B data \emph{improves} classification on the original five generators (+0.9\,pp to 0.809), indicating that cross-scale diversity benefits rather than dilutes the training signal.

\paragraph{Cross-family generalization.}
Family-level leave-out (all Pythia generators held out, trained on OLMo + Qwen only) yields $\Delta$\,=\,+0.011 F1 relative to same-family LOGO, confirming that depth features transfer across architectural families without degradation.

\paragraph{Length confound control.}
Text length correlates weakly with depth (Spearman $|\rho| < 0.14$).
Length-normalized feature trends are preserved, and length-matched subsampling yields comparable or higher F1 ($\Delta$\,=\,+0.041), ruling out length as a confound (Appendix~\ref{app:length}).


\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{llcc}
\toprule
\textbf{Generator} & \textbf{Family} & \textbf{Params} & \textbf{Held-out F1} \\
\midrule
Pythia-1B       & Pythia & 1.0B & 0.855 \\
Pythia-2.8B     & Pythia & 2.8B & 0.804 \\
OLMo-2-1B      & OLMo   & 1.5B & 0.762 \\
Qwen3-0.6B     & Qwen   & 0.6B & 0.823 \\
Qwen3-1.7B     & Qwen   & 1.7B & 0.809 \\
Qwen3-8B       & Qwen   & 8.2B & 0.685 \\
\midrule
\multicolumn{3}{l}{Average (6-gen LOGO)} & 0.790 \\
\multicolumn{3}{l}{Average (5-gen, $\leq$2.8B)} & 0.804 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Leave-one-generator-out macro-F1 for 3-class depth estimation using the 7-feature ensemble. Each row holds out one generator for testing and trains on the remaining five. The 6-gen LOGO average (0.790, 95\% CI [0.786, 0.799]) includes Qwen3-8B, whose cross-scale transfer gap lowers the mean.}
\label{tab:logo-results}
\end{table}


\subsection{Differential Depth Response}
\label{sec:results-differential}

Features exhibit \emph{differential depth response}: central-tendency and diversity measures drift monotonically with depth, while distributional shape measures remain near-stationary.
This pattern is consistent with recursive generation inducing a location shift in the token-level NLL distribution---the text becomes progressively more predictable (mean shifts), while the functional form of the distribution is preserved (shape is invariant).

Individual-level Spearman correlations with depth confirm the split (Figure~\ref{fig:feature-drift}):
drifting features show strong monotonic trends (hapax ratio $\rho = -0.558$, TTR $\rho = -0.543$, entropy mean $\rho = -0.476$),
while shape features show weak or negligible correlations (entropy std $|\rho| = 0.076$, tail decay $|\rho| = 0.087$).

\paragraph{Feature complementarity.}
Table~\ref{tab:ablation} reports ablation results.
The full 7-feature set (F1\,=\,0.790) significantly outperforms both surface-only features (TTR + hapax; F1\,=\,0.729) and reference-only features (entropy statistics + tail decay; F1\,=\,0.745; McNemar $p \approx 0$).
Permutation importance ranks hapax ratio highest (0.271), followed by TTR (0.165) and entropy mean (0.156).
Surface features capture vocabulary impoverishment; reference features capture distributional shift---neither subsumes the other.

\paragraph{Cross-family reference models.}
To confirm that differential depth response is not an artifact of the Pythia-410M reference model, we compute features using three cross-family references: Pythia-410M, OLMo-2-1B, and Qwen3-0.6B.
All three achieve LOGO F1 between 0.80 and 0.82, with consistent drift directions across features.
The pattern generalizes across reference model architectures.


\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{lcc}
\toprule
\textbf{Feature set} & \textbf{LOGO F1} & \textbf{Top feature (importance)} \\
\midrule
Full (7 features)     & 0.790 & hapax\_ratio (0.271) \\
Surface only (2)      & 0.729 & hapax\_ratio (0.320) \\
Reference only (5)    & 0.745 & entropy\_mean (0.218) \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Feature ablation (6-gen LOGO). Full $>$ surface = reference confirms complementarity between surface diversity features and reference-model distributional features.}
\label{tab:ablation}
\end{table}


\subsection{Comparison with Detection Baselines}
\label{sec:results-baselines}

We repurpose four existing detection scores as ordinal depth predictors by training the same ordinal classifier on each score as a single feature, using identical LOGO evaluation (Figure~\ref{fig:baseline-ci}).

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{lcc}
\toprule
\textbf{Method} & \textbf{LOGO F1} & \textbf{95\% CI} \\
\midrule
7-feature ensemble & \textbf{0.798} & [0.786, 0.799] \\
Avg-LogProb        & 0.765 & [0.616, 0.820] \\
LD-Score            & 0.721 & [0.588, 0.770] \\
FastDetectGPT       & 0.627 & [0.511, 0.762] \\
Binoculars          & 0.579 & [0.405, 0.664] \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Ordinal depth classification: 7-feature ensemble vs.\ single detection baselines (5-gen LOGO). The ensemble outperforms the best single detector (Avg-LogProb) by +3.9\,pp (paired bootstrap $p < 0.001$, $\Delta$ CI [3.4, 4.4]).}
\label{tab:baselines}
\end{table}

The ensemble outperforms all baselines in mean F1: +3.9\,pp over Avg-LogProb ($p < 0.001$, $\Delta$ CI [3.4, 4.4]), +7.7\,pp over LD-Score, +17.1\,pp over FastDetectGPT, and +21.9\,pp over Binoculars (Table~\ref{tab:baselines}).

The critical distinction is \emph{reliability}.
The ensemble CI spans just 1.3\,pp [0.786, 0.799], while single-detector CIs span 18--26\,pp (e.g., Avg-LogProb [0.616, 0.820]).
A single detector's CI is wider than \emph{all pairwise detector differences}, meaning no single detector is reliably best across generators.
Each detector captures partial depth signal---Avg-LogProb tracks mean perplexity shift, LD-Score captures character-level distributional change---but each fails on specific generator families.
The 7-feature ensemble aggregates complementary signals, producing stable performance regardless of the held-out generator.


\subsection{Downstream Utility: A Negative Finding}
\label{sec:results-downstream}

Can depth-aware data curation improve downstream language model quality?
We fine-tune OLMo-2-0425-1B on five data variants (3 seeds each) and evaluate perplexity on a held-out test set (Table~\ref{tab:downstream}).

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{lrc}
\toprule
\textbf{Variant} & \textbf{$n$} & \textbf{Test PPL} \\
\midrule
All depths            & 12{,}299 & 2.335 $\pm$ 0.000 \\
Size-matched (random) & 3{,}951  & 2.367 $\pm$ 0.000 \\
Depth 0--1 only       & 3{,}951  & 2.387 $\pm$ 0.001 \\
Binary-filtered       & 3{,}951  & 2.389 $\pm$ 0.000 \\
Depth 0 only          & 797      & 2.681 $\pm$ 0.001 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Downstream fine-tuning perplexity (OLMo-2-0425-1B, mean $\pm$ std across 3 seeds). At equal sample count, random subsampling (2.367) outperforms depth-aware curation (depth 0--1: 2.387, binary-filtered: 2.389).}
\label{tab:downstream}
\end{table}

The results are unambiguous: data quantity dominates depth composition.
Training on all 12{,}299 samples yields the lowest perplexity (2.335).
At equal sample count ($n$\,=\,3{,}951), random subsampling (2.367) \emph{outperforms} both depth-stratified selection (depth 0--1: 2.387) and binary detection filtering (2.389).
Cross-seed variance is below 0.002 across all variants, confirming the robustness of this null result.

Restricting training to human-only text (depth 0, $n$\,=\,797) produces a sharp perplexity increase to 2.681, driven primarily by the 5$\times$ reduction in data volume rather than depth composition per se.

We report this negative finding transparently: depth fingerprinting is an effective \emph{diagnostic} tool for characterizing text provenance, not a \emph{curative} tool for data curation.
Knowing the generation depth of a document does not, by itself, make it more or less useful for training.

\section{Related Work}
\label{sec:related}

\subsection{AI-Generated Text Detection}
\label{sec:related-detection}

Methods for distinguishing human-written from machine-generated text have evolved from statistical tests on token-level distributions \cite{gltr,grover,release_strategies} to zero-shot approaches exploiting reference-model likelihoods \cite{detectgpt,fast_detectgpt,binoculars,dna_gpt} and learned classifiers over linguistic features \cite{feat_aug_transformer,reliable_detection,ld_score}.
Recent work has pursued diverse detection signals: \citet{intrinsic_dimension} use intrinsic dimensionality estimates, \citet{diveye} propose surprisal diversity features directly comparable to our shape-based measures, and \citet{generator_barrier} characterize the distributional gap between human and model outputs.
\citet{jawahar_survey} provide a comprehensive survey.
A persistent limitation is that all these methods produce binary (real vs.\ synthetic) decisions.
Even when detection scores correlate with generation depth, they exhibit high cross-generator variance when repurposed as ordinal predictors (CI spanning 0.59--0.82 in macro-F1; \S\ref{sec:baselines}), because each score captures a single distributional property that generalizes inconsistently.
\citet{paraphrase_evades} and \citet{detection_possibilities} further demonstrate that detection robustness degrades under distributional shift.
Our reference-model entropy features are functionally NLL-based out-of-distribution scores \cite{ood_baseline}; the contribution is not a new detection method but the task formulation (ordinal depth estimation) and the empirical finding that combining drifting and stationary features yields consistent cross-generator performance.

\subsection{Model Collapse and Iterative Generation}
\label{sec:related-collapse}

A growing body of work studies quality degradation when models are trained on their own outputs.
\citet{self_consuming_mad} demonstrate that self-consuming generative models progressively lose distributional coverage, and \citet{curse_of_recursion} show that model collapse is inevitable in successive fine-tuning rounds without fresh human data, though \citet{model_collapse_avoidable} identify conditions under which careful data mixing can mitigate this effect.
\citet{strong_model_collapse} extend these results to larger-scale settings.
These studies focus on \emph{training-loop} degradation, where model weights are updated on recursive data.
Our setting is different: we study \emph{inference chains}, where a fixed model generates text conditioned on its own prior output without retraining.

Two concurrent lines of work are most directly relevant.
\citet{broken_telephone} analyze paraphrasing and translation chains, showing progressive information loss analogous to the telephone game.
\citet{markovian_chains} provide a theoretical framework for convergence in iterative text transformations, demonstrating that semantic-preservation constraints induce attractor dynamics that bound distinguishable depth to approximately three classes.
Our work differs in two respects: we study \emph{non-paraphrastic continuation} chains, where the absence of semantic anchoring permits richer depth signal beyond the attractor bound; and we focus on \emph{estimating} depth from text features rather than characterizing convergence behavior.

\subsection{Vocabulary Diversity and Stylometry}
\label{sec:related-diversity}

Declining lexical diversity in LLM-generated text is documented in both training \cite{curious_decline} and deployment \cite{writing_diversity} settings.
Our surface features---type-token ratio and hapax ratio---instantiate this observation for inference chains, where we show monotonic diversity decline across generation depths without any model retraining.

These features are classical stylometric measures with a long history in authorship attribution \cite{stamatatos_survey,koppel_authorship}.
\citet{uchendu_attribution} extend stylometric and neural methods to multi-class attribution of text to specific generators.
We push beyond generator identity to the \emph{depth} dimension: text from the same generator at different depths exhibits systematically different feature profiles, and these profiles generalize across generators.
Sampling strategies also affect diversity; \citet{nucleus_sampling} show that top-$p$ sampling mitigates some degeneration, but our results demonstrate that diversity still declines monotonically across recursive application of the same sampling procedure.

\subsection{Data Quality and Provenance}
\label{sec:related-provenance}

Scalable data curation relies on quality signals to filter web-crawled corpora.
\citet{dsir} select pretraining data to match a target distribution, \citet{qurating} learn quality scores from LLM judgments, and \citet{ccnet} filter Common Crawl via perplexity-based heuristics.
Generation depth is a complementary provenance signal: it characterizes \emph{how many steps removed} text is from a human source, orthogonal to content quality per se.

An alternative approach is proactive provenance through watermarking \cite{watermark_llm,synthid_text,aaronson_watermark}, where identifiable patterns are embedded during generation.
However, \citet{chainwash} demonstrate that watermark strength decays across multi-step generation chains, motivating passive post-hoc methods that do not require generator cooperation.
Our depth fingerprinting is such a method: it operates on text alone without assuming access to the generating model or an embedded watermark.
At the feature level, our reference-model NLL analysis connects to \citet{min_k_percent}, who use the probability distribution's lower tail for membership inference; we analyze the full NLL distribution for a different purpose---ordinal depth estimation rather than training-set membership.

\citet{jawahar_survey} provide a comprehensive survey.
A persistent limitation is that all these methods produce binary (real vs.\ synthetic) decisions.

\citet{paraphrase_evades} and \citet{detection_possibilities} further demonstrate that detection robustness degrades under distributional shift.

Our reference-model entropy features are functionally NLL-based out-of-distribution scores \cite{ood_baseline}; the contribution is not a new detection method but the task formulation (ordinal depth estimation) and the empirical finding that combining drifting and stationary features yields consistent cross-generator performance.
